newsitem.title: UK: Dollar/yen slump turns intervention fears on head.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/yen slump turns intervention fears on head.

text.p: Dollar/yen ended a punishing week sharply weaker, leaving the market abuzz with speculation of intervention to sell yen just weeks after the talk was all of concerted buying.
Only last week, the dollar's persistent strength sparked fears of joint intervention to dampen it, plus a chorus of yen-positive comments from Japanese officials.

The market took heed. In just 15 days, the dollar has plunged almost 13 yen. "It's incredible that only a few weeks ago they were trying to achieve the opposite," said Peter von Maydell, senior currency strategist at UBS in London.
The dollar was quoted at 115.51/55 yen at 1531 GMT, down from late Thursday's European level of 116.20/35 but well off an intrasession low of 114.87.
Dollar/yen's sharp bounce from that level came amid market talk of Bank of England buying on behalf of the Bank of Japan, but there was no confirmation and traders were sceptical.

"Even if they do want dollar/yen lower, they'll be more than happy to see it settle around current levels for a while to at least give some semblance of stability, which is what the G7 communique was about after all," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist for Europe at Bank of America here.

In the communique issued after its late April meeting in Washington, the Group of Seven said excessive volatility and deviations from fundamentals were undesirable, and vowed to cooperate in the forex markets as appropriate.

Japanese vice finance minister Takatoshi Kato said today the markets had now fully absorbed the G7 accord. However, he kept alive the prospect of higher Japanese interest rates by saying the economic recovery was intact and private demand rising.
The market's stampede into yen was vivdly illustrated by mark/yen, which skidded to a 20-month low of 67.73 during the session from 68.35/38 in late Europe on Thursday.
It had recovered to 68.17/20 by 1609 GMT, however, leaving dollar/mark languishing at a session low of 1.6908/13 -- down from yesterday's close here of 1.6990/00.

All the same, dollar/mark was largely subdued in Europe as the yen hogged the limelight. It was supported by growing speculation of a broad-based European monetary union, usually seen as conducive to a softer euro and negative for the mark.

"When you do see dollar/mark moving down, on the whole it doesn't have much impact on the mark crosses within the ERM. That tells you something about the market's lack of willingness to buy the mark," said BankAmerica's Hawkins.
With the policy-making U.S. Federal Open Market Committee due to meet on Tuesday, interest rate differentials remained at the forefront of market minds.
U.S. data out today outstripped consensus expectations, but analysts said the market remains deeply uncertain whether the Fed will tighten again so soon after the rate hike on March 25.
The University of Michigan May sentiment survey came in at 104.6, above April's 101.4 and the predicted 101.6. Analysts noted the expectations index rose to 98.6 from 92.5.
April housing starts increased by 2.6 percent to 1.473 million units, overshooting forecasts of 1.4 million.
Farther afield, emerging currencies like the Thai baht and Czech crown suffered again today, prompting heavy central bank intervention and higher interest rates.
The rise in the yen and long-term Japanese interest rates have prompted a retreat of both Japanese and yen-funded capital around the world, hammering many emerging market currencies.

Analysts said economic slowdown and consequent thoughts of lower interest rates in some emerging markets had spooked speculative investors thirsty for high yields, especially amid talk of Japanese tightening.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
